name: CI-based regression testing for LLM/agent evaluation (schedule- and change-triggered eval re-runs)
what_it_is: A pattern where an LLM/agent evaluation suite is wired into CI so it re-runs automatically and fails the build (or opens a report) when quality regresses. Four concrete precedents: (1) promptfoo runs a declarative eval suite (promptfooconfig.yaml) as a GitHub Action, triggered on pull_request with a paths filter, doing a before/after diff of edited prompts and posting results back on the PR; it also documents a nightly `schedule: cron` variant to catch provider-side model drift. (2) DeepEval writes evals as pytest tests via assert_test() and runs them with `deepeval test run` as a CI step, failing the build when any metric drops below its threshold. (3) garak (NVIDIA) is a CLI LLM vulnerability scanner (probes for jailbreaks, injection, leakage) that runs against a target model from the command line and produces a report. (4) The general community pattern splits eval suites into smoke / PR / nightly / release tiers, running ~10 cases per PR and 100+ on a daily cron. The unifying idea: treat model+prompt quality like code that can silently regress, and gate/alert on it.
real_precedent: promptfoo (promptfoo/promptfoo-action GitHub Action; docs at promptfoo.dev); DeepEval (confident-ai/deepeval, docs deepeval.com); garak (NVIDIA/garak); plus the tiered smoke/PR/nightly/release cron pattern documented in practitioner writeups. Each is a real, shipped project, not an invented example.
evidence_of_impact: garak has 8.6k GitHub stars, is Apache-2.0, was described as the leading LLM vulnerability scanner in a 2024 Fujitsu Research review, and is used/recommended by Microsoft, Trend Micro, NVIDIA and Cisco (per the NVIDIA/garak README and Wikipedia). promptfoo is a widely referenced open-source (MIT) eval CLI with a dedicated GitHub Action and extensive CI/CD docs; the promptfoo-action repo itself shows 69 stars / 32 forks [uncertain] (the core promptfoo repo star count was not independently fetched). DeepEval bills itself as the pytest-for-LLMs framework with native pytest + GitHub Actions integration and documented CI/CD regression guides. Concrete adoption/user counts for promptfoo and DeepEval beyond the docs were not independently verified. [uncertain]
applicability_to_agentdyno: Build a `dyno ci` reusable GitHub Action (or a documented workflow snippet) that wraps `dyno doctor --json` and gates on regressions. Trigger it three ways, matching the precedents: (a) `schedule: cron` nightly/weekly (promptfoo's drift-catching pattern), (b) `workflow_dispatch` for manual re-runs, and (c) a `paths` filter on a committed manifest that pins the model file, llama.cpp version, and Ollama version -- so bumping any of those three re-runs the doctor exam automatically (the stated goal). The action stores a baseline doctor result (grade A-F + per-tool-call pass/fail) as a committed JSON artifact, then diffs the new run against it and fails / opens an issue when the grade drops or a tool-calling test flips pass->fail -- exactly DeepEval's assert-below-threshold-fails-the-build discipline and promptfoo's before/after PR diff, but the 'thresholds' are AgentDyno's own doctor grades. The one architectural twist that makes this genuinely differentiated: promptfoo/DeepEval run on `ubuntu-latest` hitting cloud APIs, whereas AgentDyno's exam runs against a local llama-server/Ollama on 127.0.0.1:8403, so the workflow must target a self-hosted runner with real GPU/CPU hardware. That is the moat -- 'CI that re-runs a real local hardware exam on model/backend version change' has no direct precedent; promptfoo, DeepEval and garak all assume a remotely reachable model endpoint, not a local weights-plus-runtime bundle whose behavior changes when llama.cpp or Ollama is upgraded.
build_effort: medium. `dyno doctor` already produces the exam result and AgentDyno already has a stable local gateway, so the new surface is: (1) a `--json` machine-readable doctor output with a stable schema if not already present (small), (2) a `dyno ci` subcommand or a composite GitHub Action that runs doctor, loads a committed baseline, diffs grades/tool-call results, and sets exit code + writes a PR comment / GitHub step summary (medium), and (3) documentation + an example workflow using self-hosted runner, schedule cron, workflow_dispatch, and a paths filter on the pinned-versions manifest (small). The genuinely non-trivial part is the self-hosted-runner requirement and defining a stable, low-noise regression signal from an inherently stochastic exam.
risk_or_caveat: 1) Non-determinism: local model sampling makes A-F grades and tool-call pass/fail noisy, so naive diffing produces flaky red builds -- needs fixed seeds/temperature, repeats, and tolerance bands (DeepEval exposes repeats/flags for exactly this reason). 2) Self-hosted-runner friction: unlike promptfoo/DeepEval which run free on ubuntu-latest cloud runners, AgentDyno's exam needs real local hardware, so users must stand up and maintain a self-hosted runner -- a real adoption barrier and a support burden. 3) Scope overlap: promptfoo already does red-team + eval-in-CI and garak already does scheduled-style vuln scanning against ggml/gguf and REST targets, so AgentDyno must stay tightly scoped to the hardware-fit + agentic tool-calling regression niche rather than becoming a generic eval-in-CI tool. 4) Baseline maintenance: someone must curate and update the committed baseline as legitimate model upgrades change grades, or every intended improvement reads as a regression.
